name: Timeouts, Circuit Breakers and Fallbacks
question: What does the agent do when a provider slows down or fails?
summary: Give every model and tool call a timeout shorter than the user’s patience, stop calling a dependency that keeps failing with a circuit breaker (closed, open, half-open), and route to a fallback: a second provider, a smaller model, a cached answer or a clear message. Panel 8 makes one call safe to retry; this protects the whole system when a dependency degrades.
useCases: Any dependency on a hosted model or external API
Traffic high enough that hung calls can exhaust workers

items.detail: per call, well below the end-to-end target; the Anthropic and OpenAI Python SDKs default to 10 minutes
the same SDKs retry 2 times by default; add jitter and a retry budget
closed → open after N failures → half-open probe → closed
secondary provider, smaller model, cached answer, graceful message
a separate concurrency limit per dependency
busy workers = request rate × average time per request

steps: Set explicit timeouts and retry counts on every client
Wrap each dependency in a circuit breaker
Define and test a fallback for each critical call
Run outage drills: inject latency and errors, and watch the whole system
pitfalls: Default 10-minute timeouts let hung calls exhaust every worker
Retries without a budget multiply load on a provider that is already failing
Fallback paths that were never tested fail on the day they are needed
remember: Short timeouts, fail fast, always have a plan B.
caption: Illustrative: a breaker opens after 5 failures, probes after 30 s and sends traffic to a fallback while open.

code.text: pass                          # open: primary skipped, no wait
return cached_or_message(q)   # cached answer or a clear note

steps.title: Set a timeout on every client
steps.text: Both SDKs wait up to 10 minutes by default. At 20 requests a second, hung calls would hold thousands of workers; 8 seconds bounds the damage.

steps.title: Keep the retry budget small
steps.text: The SDKs retry twice by default. One retry on the primary and none on the fallback stops a slow provider from receiving three times the load.

steps.title: Wrap the dependency in a breaker
steps.text: pybreaker counts failures. After 5 in a row it opens and stops calling the primary for 30 seconds, then lets one probe through.

steps.title: Fall back to a second provider
steps.text: When the primary fails or is skipped, the same question goes to a second provider with its own timeout. Test this path before you need it.

steps.title: Fail fast while open
steps.text: An open breaker raises immediately, so requests skip the 8-second wait and go straight to the fallback. Latency stays low during the outage.

steps.title: Have a last resort
steps.text: If both providers fail, return a cached answer or a clear message instead of an error page or a hung request.

pros: One slow provider no longer takes down the whole service
Users get an answer or a clear message, fast
Load on a failing dependency drops, which helps it recover
cons: Fallback models answer differently, so evaluate them too
Short timeouts can cut off slow but healthy calls
Breakers need tuning to avoid flapping
avoidWhen: Adding retries without timeouts or a budget: that multiplies the load
Falling back to a model that was never evaluated on your task

playgroundGuide.scenario: A stockbroker’s order-support assistant serves 20 requests a second from a pool of 200 workers. For 20 minutes its primary model provider hangs on 40% of calls; healthy calls take 2 s. Set the timeout, retries, circuit breaker and fallback, and see whether the service stays up.
controls: Pick the timeout per call, from the 600 s SDK default down to 3 s.
Pick the retries on the primary, and tick the circuit breaker.
Pick a fallback: none, a secondary provider or a cached answer, or load a scenario.

outputs.name: Requests answered well
outputs.meaning: Share of requests that get a good answer during the outage, after any saturation.

outputs.name: p95 latency
outputs.meaning: The time within which 95% of requests finish.

outputs.name: Busy workers
outputs.meaning: Request rate × average time per request (Little’s law), against the pool of 200.

presets.name: SDK defaults, no fallback
presets.expect: 7,525 busy workers against a pool of 200: the service is down, 2.5% answered.

presets.name: 8 s timeout, 1 retry
presets.expect: 123 busy workers, 84% answered: failures now reach users, p95 16 s.

presets.name: Plus a secondary provider
presets.expect: 99.5% answered, but p95 is 19 s because failures wait for timeouts first.

missions.text: Answer at least 95% of requests well during the outage.
missions.hint: Timeouts keep workers free; a fallback turns failures into answers.

missions.text: Answer at least 95% well with p95 latency under 8 seconds.
missions.hint: Stop waiting on the failing provider: a breaker, or a very short timeout.

missions.text: With no fallback at all, keep busy workers under the pool of 200.
missions.hint: Bound how long a hung call can hold a worker.

practice.scenario: A stockbroker’s order-support assistant sees about 20 requests a second at market open. When its primary model provider slowed down, SDK calls with the default 10-minute timeout held every worker, and the whole assistant went down. Now each call times out after 8 seconds, a router falls back to a second provider, and a cooldown takes the failing deployment out of rotation.

industries.use: Keep order-status answers flowing at market open when one provider degrades
Fail fast to a clear message when a bank API is down instead of holding threads
Fall back to a smaller model for rebooking chat during a provider outage

practice.analogy: A circuit breaker in your house. When a fault keeps tripping, it cuts the line so the fault cannot burn down everything else.

library.name: LiteLLM Router
library.what: One interface over many providers, with per-call timeouts, retries, fallbacks and cooldowns for failing deployments.

practice.note: Test the fallback path in drills; a fallback that has never run is a guess.

samples.code:
from litellm import Router

router = Router(
    model_list=[
        {"model_name": "primary",
         "litellm_params": {"model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929", "timeout": 8}},
        {"model_name": "secondary",
         "litellm_params": {"model": "openai/gpt-4o-2024-08-06", "timeout": 8}},
    ],
    fallbacks=[{"primary": ["secondary"]}],   # used after primary fails
    num_retries=1,                            # small retry budget
    allowed_fails=3,                          # failures before cooldown
    cooldown_time=30,                         # seconds out of rotation
)

def answer(question: str) -> str:
    try:
        r = router.completion(model="primary",
                              messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}])
        return r.choices[0].message.content
    except Exception:
        return "Order status is delayed right now. Please check the order book in the app."

numericDrill.question: An assistant receives 20 requests a second. During a provider slowdown the average request takes 12 seconds. By Little’s law, how many requests are in flight at once, and does that fit a pool of 200 workers?
numericDrill.answer: In flight = 20 × 12 = 240, which is more than the pool of 200, so requests queue and time out and the whole service degrades. An 8-second timeout with a fast fallback keeps the average near 3 s: 20 × 3 = 60 in flight.

interview.question: What are the three states of a circuit breaker?
interview.answer: Closed: calls pass through and failures are counted. Open: after a failure threshold, calls fail immediately or go to a fallback, without touching the dependency. Half-open: after a cooldown, a trial call is let through; success closes the breaker, failure opens it again.

interview.question: Why can retries make an outage worse?
interview.answer: Each retry adds load to a dependency that is already struggling, and with several layers of retries the load multiplies. Use a small retry count with backoff and jitter, a retry budget as a share of traffic, and a circuit breaker so calls stop when failure is persistent.

mistakes.fix: Set a timeout per call below your end-to-end target

mistakes.mistake: Adding a fallback that has never been exercised
mistakes.fix: Run failure drills that force traffic onto the fallback

quiz.question: An order-support assistant receives 50 requests a second, each taking 4 s on average. By Little’s law, how many are in flight at once?
quiz.explanation: 50 × 4 = 200 requests in flight.

quiz.question: A service has a pool of 300 workers and 30 requests a second. What is the highest average request time it can sustain?
quiz.explanation: 300 ÷ 30 = 10 s; any longer and requests queue.

quiz.question: The Anthropic and OpenAI Python SDKs, left at defaults, time out after how long?
quiz.explanation: Both default to 10 minutes, far longer than most user-facing targets.

quiz.question: Three layers each retry a failed call twice, three attempts per layer. In the worst case, how many attempts reach the provider for one user request?
quiz.explanation: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 attempts: retries multiply across layers.

quiz.question: Which belong in a safe retry policy? Select all that apply.
options: A small retry budget as a share of traffic
Retrying every error immediately in a tight loop
quiz.explanation: Backoff, jitter and budgets limit load; immediate retries and retrying bad requests add it.

quiz.question: What does a circuit breaker do after the failure threshold is reached?
options: Opens and fails fast without calling the dependency, then probes after a cooldown
quiz.explanation: Open means skip the dependency; half-open lets a probe test recovery.

quiz.question: In the half-open state, a probe call succeeds. What happens?
options: The breaker closes and normal calls resume
All requests go to the fallback
quiz.explanation: A successful probe closes the breaker.

quiz.question: Primary calls fail 40% of the time during an outage. With 2 retries (3 attempts) and independent failures, what share of requests fail every attempt?
quiz.explanation: 0.4³ = 0.064, so 6.4% still fail after three attempts.

quiz.question: During a provider outage, which changes lower p95 latency for users? Select all that apply.
options: A circuit breaker that skips the failing provider
More retries on the failing provider
quiz.explanation: Skipping the failure and bounding waits cut latency; retries and long timeouts add to it.

quiz.question: A symptom-checker falls back to a smaller model during outages. What must be true before relying on it?
options: The fallback has been evaluated on the task and exercised in drills
It must be from the same provider
It must be larger than the primary
quiz.explanation: Untested fallbacks answer differently and may fail on the day they are needed.

quiz.question: What is a bulkhead in resilience design?
options: A separate concurrency limit per dependency, so one slow dependency cannot use every worker
quiz.explanation: Bulkheads isolate failures by capping resources per dependency.

quiz.question: At market open a provider slows down and the whole order assistant goes down. Which are likely contributing causes? Select all that apply.
options: Retries multiplied load on the struggling provider
quiz.explanation: Long waits exhaust workers and retries amplify load; prompt length and batch export are not causes.

quiz.question: A 3-second timeout cuts off 10% of healthy calls that take a little longer. What is the trade-off?
options: No trade-off; shorter is always better
Shorter timeouts free workers faster but turn slow successes into failures
quiz.explanation: Set timeouts from the latency distribution of healthy calls, not as low as possible.

quiz.question: When both the primary and the secondary provider fail, what should a customer-facing agent return?
options: A cached answer or a clear message about the delay
quiz.explanation: A graceful last resort beats an error page or a hung request.

quiz.question: Which tools provide cross-provider fallbacks for model calls? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: LiteLLM and Portkey route between providers with fallbacks; the others handle drift and prompt versions.

quiz.question: In LiteLLM’s Router, what does a cooldown do?
options: Takes a deployment that keeps failing out of rotation for a period
quiz.explanation: Failing deployments are skipped for the cooldown time, similar to an open breaker.

quiz.question: A pybreaker breaker is configured with fail_max=5, reset_timeout=30. What does this mean?
options: Open after 5 consecutive failures and try again after 30 seconds
quiz.explanation: fail_max is the failure threshold; reset_timeout is the cooldown before a probe.

quiz.question: An outage drill injects 40% errors into the primary provider. What should the team measure? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Drills check whether users still get good, timely answers and whether capacity holds.

quiz.question: Why should a retried payment tool call carry an idempotency key even behind a circuit breaker?
options: A timed-out call may still have succeeded, so a retry could pay twice
quiz.explanation: Timeouts do not mean failure on the other side; keys make retries safe.

quiz.question: Which designs keep an assistant up when its only model provider degrades? Select all that apply.
options: Short timeouts and a small retry budget
A circuit breaker with a tested fallback
More workers with the same 10-minute timeout
Retrying every failed call five times
quiz.explanation: Bounded waits and fail-fast fallbacks protect capacity; more workers and more retries only delay the collapse.
